notes.text: I'm opening the mission briefing to see what the task involves.

I'm sizing up the problem: six unknowns, and each test drop reveals the impact point, fall time, whether it lands in smoke, and the wind at that altitude, all with some noise. Dropping at different heights should let me build up a rough picture of how the wind changes with altitude.

I'm weighing where to place the first drop: an altitude around 100 m gives a fall time of roughly 4.5 seconds, but drag changes that, since the load's falling speed levels off depending on the drag coefficient. I'm also considering whether the smoke column might carry an updraft that would lengthen the fall and shift the impact point.

I'm settling on a first test drop away from the smoke, at x=0, y=-300, from altitude 100 m with heading 0 and speed 60, so that any wind drift is unlikely to pull the load into the updraft.

I'm working out the wind at 100 m, about 6.2 m/s toward 32°. The fall takes 7.13 s, longer than free fall would, so drag matters here. The aircraft's northward drift comes out to about 106 m rather than the 428 m I'd expect, so I'm checking how the horizontal velocity settles toward the air's motion.

The drift is far short of the 428 m a free-falling load would cover, so the air is clearly pulling the horizontal velocity toward its own. I'm now planning a second drop from 30 m at the same heading and speed, since a shorter fall should show the drag more cleanly with less wind influence.

Now I'm working out the wind shear exponent from the speed ratio between 30 m and 100 m, which comes out to about 0.28. The 0.5 m/s noise means the estimate will be rough, and I'm checking the veer next.

I'm checking the veer estimate, which is about -31 degrees per 100 m with roughly ±8 degrees of uncertainty from the noise. The fall time of 3.29 s is well above the 2.47 s free-fall value from 30 m, so drag is clearly a factor. I'm planning a 150 m drop on the same heading to get more of the wind profile and a second fall time.

Now I'm checking the wind speeds at each height against the shear exponent, trying to pin down a value that fits the noisy data, and I'm starting to sketch out how the direction veers with height.

Now I'm working out the vertical veer per 100 m with a linear fit across the three heights, which comes out to roughly -25 degrees per 100 m. Then I'm turning to the drag: the fall times from 150 m, 100 m and 30 m are the reference points I'll need for fitting.

Now I'm estimating the drag coefficient from the fall times, starting with the 30 m drop that takes 3.29 s against 2.47 s in free fall, and modelling vertical speed with a quadratic drag term.

I'm checking whether a higher drag coefficient gets the 30 m fall to 3.29 s, but the first attempt comes out too quick, so the direction of the drag effect needs rechecking.

I'm checking the drag numbers now: a drag coefficient near 0.06 seems to reproduce the 30 m fall time of 3.29 s, since the 0.03 case comes out too quick.

Checking the drag fit: at k around 0.063, the 30 m fall lands near 3.29 s. The horizontal relative speed is large, but it stays out of the vertical drag estimate here.

Now I'm sizing up how the horizontal wind relative speed feeds into the vertical drag, since it's large early on and the simple estimate probably understates it, so I'll need a numerical simulation to check the fall times.

Next I'm picking a drag coefficient of about 0.06 to test against the drops, with the updraft left at zero since none of these drops entered the smoke. I'm also setting the initial horizontal velocity to 60 m/s along heading zero.

I'm checking the predicted fall times against the observed ones, and the 100 m case shows the prediction running about 2 seconds long. That points to drag being overestimated. The 150 m test shows the same gap, so the error looks consistent rather than a one-off.

I'm going to try a lower drag coefficient, around 0.03. I also notice the y residual is negative, which would mean the prediction lands farther south, but with less drag the horizontal velocity should hold closer to 60 and carry it farther north, so I'll check whether that fixes it.

I'm weighing whether a slightly lower drag coefficient, around 0.027, would fit better, since the residuals at 0.03 predict too long a time at 150 m. I'm also estimating how sensitive that residual is to k, which looks roughly linear at about 100 seconds per unit of drag.

I'm settling on a drag coefficient near 0.028, since the timing residuals from different tests point to slightly different zeros and I'm treating the gap as noise. Next I'm turning to the wind, where the impact residuals suggest a small adjustment, and I'll see whether a modest reduction in drag shifts them much.

I'm working out the updraft: a load dropped straight over the fire would pass through the smoke column, and the updraft would slow its fall, so the fall time should reveal the updraft's strength. Since the targets have different intensities, I'm also noting that the updraft's size scales with intensity and its radius scales with its square root.

I'm considering a test drop straight through the smoke column at the fire's center, so I can measure the updraft from how much the fall time stretches. To land near (0,0) from 150 m, I'd release at roughly (-25, -124) heading 0 at 60 m/s, though the updraft will shift that somewhat.

I'm picking a release point for a calibration drop at the fire's center, starting from about 100 m altitude so the updraft's effect on fall time is easier to read. I'm estimating that releasing near (-20, -106) should land close to the origin, with the updraft shifting it somewhat.

I'm going to go ahead and run the calibration drop now rather than tune the drag coefficient any further.
I've entered the smoke, and the fall time of 8.35 is longer than the roughly 7.1 I'd predict with no updraft. I'll test updraft hypotheses against the measured wind, starting with an updraft of 5.
The test 4 prediction comes out 0.17 seconds short of the observation, which suggests the updraft is too weak, so I'll try raising it to around 7.

I'm checking the residual for test 4 with updraft 7, which comes out at +0.45, against -0.17 at updraft 5. Interpolating between those puts the zero near 5.55 m/s, with the slope at about 0.31 per m/s. The noise on dt is around 0.05, so that estimate is only approximate. Next I'm turning to the dx and dy residuals.

I'm weighing whether the dy residuals at updraft 5 and 7 point to a different updraft or to something else in the wind model. Given four drops, my estimates for k, the updraft, and the wind speed and direction are only roughly settled, so I'm now looking at how the wind parameters, shear and veer, would change the impact at different altitudes.

I'm checking the wind parameters against the direct measurements: the speed and direction at 30, 100 and 150 m fit a shear exponent around 0.15, and the veer comes out near -25 per 100 m. With six drops left, I'd rather use them to test different altitudes and headings than keep refining these numbers from the same data.

I'm settling on the test drops as the way to check the model: a fast drop from a different heading and altitude will show whether the wind and drag terms hold up away from the calibration set, and I have six of them left to spend on that.

I'm settling on a test drop from a different heading and a higher speed, starting from around (300, 0) at 50 m altitude, so the drag and wind terms get checked in a regime the calibration set didn't cover.

I'm going to release the next test drop from around (400, 0) with a heading of 270 and see where it lands, though I can't yet say exactly how far west it will end up.

Checking wind speed at 50 m against the other heights, I get about 4.4 at 49°, and the shear exponent comes out near 0.45, though the data are noisy. The fall takes 4.4 s from 50 m, with impact around (334.9, 11.6).

I'm comparing the displacement of about (-65, +11.6) against the hypothesis I'm testing.

I'm checking whether the test 5 residual of 2.6 in dx means the prediction landed more east than the observation, and I'm sorting out the direction of the wind's push against the observed westward drift.

I'm working out whether the wind speed at 50 m is actually lower than the model assumed, since the 4.4 measurement is weaker than the 5.3 the 0.15 shear predicted. That would fit the observed westward drift, and I'm testing whether a steeper shear profile explains the data better than the current fit.

I'm trying shear 0.15 with W=6.0 and getting predictions of 5.0 at 30 m and 5.4 at 50 m, which both fall short of the 4.4 measurements. I'm checking whether a larger shear with a higher W does better, and starting with shear 0.4 at W=6.2 gives 3.8 at 30 m and 4.7 at 50 m.

I'm fitting the shear and reference speed to the four height measurements, and the 150 m sample is an outlier at either fit. I'm trying s=0.3 with W=6.1, which fits the 30 and 50 m points somewhat better, but the residuals are still uneven.

I'm checking whether a veer of about -20 with the direction near 36 degrees fits the measured wind directions better than the current -25 setup, since the 30 m and 150 m points are the ones that drift furthest off. I'm also keeping shear 0.3 and wind 6.1 and testing that combination against the impact residuals.

I'm now trying a shear of 0.3 to see how it changes the fit.

Checking the residuals now: the x-direction errors are small, while the y-direction ones swing more, with test 2 showing the largest miss at -3.5. I suspect drag is playing into that north-going velocity, and both early y residuals lean negative.

I'm weighing whether to lower the drag coefficient, since the negative y residuals on tests 1 and 2 point toward less drag, but test 3's positive time residual argues the other way. Given the 1.5 m noise, these misses look like they fall within normal scatter, so the fit may already be close. I'm leaning toward spending some of the remaining test drops at other altitudes and headings to check the model where operations will actually run.

I'm going to use the 150 m drop through the smoke column to pin down the updraft speed, since a higher release gives the load more time in the rising air. The earlier 100 m drop put the best fit near 5.5, and the test 4 residuals support that same value.

I'm settling on a 150 m release heading 90 at speed 70, so the drop passes through the middle of the smoke column at a height where the updraft has time to act. I'll simulate that first to find a release point that lands on the target.

I'm going to simulate from (-100, 0) to see where that release lands before settling on it.

I'm working out where to release from so the impact lands at the origin, given that the wind is uniform and the updraft column is fixed at the fire, so the displacement only depends on the release point through relative positions.

I'm settling on a release point of about (-113.8, -49.9) so the impact lands at the origin, and I'm noting the updraft will shift the landing somewhat, though passing through the smoke is still fine. Next I'm setting up a test drop with heading 90, altitude 150, speed 70, starting at x=-114, y=-50.
The wind has picked up to 7.1 at 31°, from 6.3 at 24° before. I'll treat that change as noise and now check it against my current hypothesis.

I'm checking test 6 by comparing the predicted impact with the observed one, and the prediction comes out a bit off. Next I plan a systematic adjustment, setting up the parameters I'll need to fit.

I'm now comparing test 6's observed displacement with the model's prediction, noting it lands further south than expected. The model's wind direction at 150 m looks too far north compared with the measured 31°, and the measured wind directions across altitudes suggest a linear trend I want to fit.

I'm fitting a linear trend to the measured wind directions, which gives about 37° at 100 m and a veer of roughly -23° per unit altitude. I'll test that with direction 36° and veer -23, and I'm also settling on a power-law speed profile with W=6.1 and s=0.3, which fits the measured speeds reasonably well.

The test 3 offset has grown to about 3.5 m as the 36 m wind pushes it further east, while test 6 has improved. Both are 150 m shots, so the split looks mixed rather than systematic. With residuals around 1.5 m and an average miss near 2 to 2.5 m, I'm wondering whether this is just noise.

The residuals look close to the noise floor, around 1.5 to 2 m per axis, with test 2 still sitting consistently about 3.5 m short in y. I'm running RMS on two candidate parameter sets, and the second one, with the wind at 36 m and the speed at -23, comes out slightly lower at about 1.95.

I'm weighing whether to lower the drag coefficient to 0.026, since that would make the test 2 y-residual less negative and bring the test 3 time residual closer to zero, while keeping D=36 and V=-23.

I'm checking the dt residuals at k 0.028 and 0.026; the mean is about +0.055 at the higher value and about -0.09 at the lower, so k near 0.0275 looks likely. I also note the dt residuals seem to depend on wind through |v_rel|, and I'm starting to feel we're close to the noise floor.

I'm weighing whether to spend the last four test drops, since more data should tighten the parameter fit. I'm thinking about drops close to the target conditions, especially at low altitude where the wind profile matters most, and I'm considering two drops at 30 m with different headings and speeds to check that.
